# Learning goals

In this lab, you are expected to learn/put into practice the following skills:

- Evaluate whether a problem can be parallelized.
- Practice using the `parallel` package.

```{r setup}
set.seed(1234)
```

## Problem 1: Vectorization

The following functions can be written more efficiently without using
parallelization. For each function, I created a faster version, verified its
output, and compared its speed with the original version.

### 1. Generating a matrix of Poisson random variables

The original function repeatedly uses `rbind()` inside a loop. This is
inefficient because R must repeatedly allocate and copy the growing matrix.
The alternative generates all values at once and places them into a matrix.

```{r p2-fun1}
fun1 <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  x <- NULL
  
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    x <- rbind(x, rpois(k, lambda))
  }
  
  return(x)
}

fun1alt <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  matrix(
    rpois(n * k, lambda),
    nrow = n,
    ncol = k,
    byrow = TRUE
  )
}
```

Both functions should produce matrices with the same dimensions.

```{r check-fun1-dimensions}
set.seed(1234)
x1 <- fun1(n = 10000, k = 4, lambda = 4)

set.seed(5678)
x1alt <- fun1alt(n = 10000, k = 4, lambda = 4)

dim(x1)
dim(x1alt)

identical(dim(x1), dim(x1alt))
```

The individual values will not necessarily be identical because they are
randomly generated. However, the values should follow similar Poisson
distributions.

```{r check-fun1-distributions}
comparison_fun1 <- data.frame(
  function_name = c("fun1", "fun1alt"),
  mean = c(mean(x1), mean(x1alt)),
  variance = c(var(as.vector(x1)), var(as.vector(x1alt))),
  minimum = c(min(x1), min(x1alt)),
  maximum = c(max(x1), max(x1alt))
)

comparison_fun1
```

Both functions produce values with means and variances close to the specified
Poisson mean of 4.

The following benchmark compares their execution speeds.

```{r benchmark-fun1}
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  original = fun1(),
  vectorized = fun1alt(),
  times = 100
)
```

The vectorized version should generally be faster because it creates the
complete matrix in one operation instead of repeatedly expanding it with
`rbind()`.

### 2. Finding the maximum value of each column

```{r p2-fun2}
# Data-generating process: 10 x 1,000 matrix
set.seed(1234)
x <- matrix(rnorm(1e4), nrow = 10)

fun2 <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, max)
}

fun2alt <- function(x) {
  do.call(
    pmax,
    lapply(seq_len(nrow(x)), function(i) x[i, ])
  )
}
```

The alternative function passes the rows of the matrix to `pmax()`.
This calculates the maximum across rows for every column.

The outputs of the two functions are identical.

```{r check-fun2-output}
output_fun2 <- fun2(x)
output_fun2alt <- fun2alt(x)

all.equal(
  unname(output_fun2),
  unname(output_fun2alt)
)

head(output_fun2)
head(output_fun2alt)
```

The execution speeds are compared below.

```{r benchmark-fun2}
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  original = fun2(x),
  vectorized = fun2alt(x),
  times = 100
)
```

The `pmax()` version avoids repeatedly calling a separate function for every
column and should generally be faster for this matrix.

## Problem 3: Parallelization

Bootstrapping involves repeating the same calculation on many independently
resampled datasets. Therefore, the bootstrap replications can be distributed
across multiple processor cores.

### 1. Parallel bootstrap function

The function below uses `parallel::mclapply()` on macOS and Linux. On Windows,
where forked processing is unavailable, it creates a PSOCK cluster and uses
`parallel::parLapply()` instead.

When `ncpus = 1L`, the function uses the original serial `lapply()` method.

```{r p3-boot-fun}
my_boot <- function(dat, stat, R, ncpus = 1L) {
  
  # Check the arguments
  stopifnot(
    is.data.frame(dat) || is.matrix(dat),
    is.function(stat),
    length(R) == 1L,
    R >= 1,
    length(ncpus) == 1L,
    ncpus >= 1
  )
  
  R <- as.integer(R)
  ncpus <- as.integer(ncpus)
  
  # Generate the bootstrap row indices
  n <- nrow(dat)
  idx <- matrix(
    sample.int(n, n * R, replace = TRUE),
    nrow = n,
    ncol = R
  )
  
  bootstrap_once <- function(i) {
    stat(dat[idx[, i], , drop = FALSE])
  }
  
  if (ncpus == 1L) {
    
    # Serial calculation
    ans <- lapply(seq_len(R), bootstrap_once)
    
  } else if (.Platform$OS.type != "windows") {
    
    # Parallel calculation for macOS and Linux
    ans <- parallel::mclapply(
      seq_len(R),
      bootstrap_once,
      mc.cores = ncpus
    )
    
  } else {
    
    # Parallel calculation for Windows
    cl <- parallel::makeCluster(ncpus)
    on.exit(parallel::stopCluster(cl), add = TRUE)
    
    parallel::clusterExport(
      cl,
      varlist = c("dat", "stat", "idx"),
      envir = environment()
    )
    
    ans <- parallel::parLapply(
      cl,
      seq_len(R),
      function(i) {
        stat(dat[idx[, i], , drop = FALSE])
      }
    )
  }
  
  # Convert the list of estimates into a matrix
  ans <- do.call(rbind, ans)
  
  return(ans)
}
```

### 2. Checking the bootstrap confidence intervals

The statistic used for this example contains the estimated intercept and slope
from an ordinary least-squares regression.

```{r p3-test-boot}
# Bootstrap statistic for an OLS regression
my_stat <- function(d) {
  coef(lm(y ~ x, data = d))
}

# Simulate the data
set.seed(1)

n <- 500
R <- 1e4

x <- rnorm(n)
y <- 5 * x + rnorm(n)

simulation_data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Parametric confidence intervals
ans0 <- confint(lm(y ~ x, data = simulation_data))

# Bootstrap estimates
set.seed(1)

ans1 <- my_boot(
  dat = simulation_data,
  stat = my_stat,
  R = R,
  ncpus = 2L
)

# Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals
ans1_ci <- t(
  apply(
    ans1,
    2,
    quantile,
    probs = c(0.025, 0.975)
  )
)

ans1_ci
ans0
```

The bootstrap confidence intervals should be similar to the parametric
confidence intervals returned by `confint()`. They will not be exactly
identical because the bootstrap procedure is based on random resampling.

### 3. Comparing serial and parallel execution

```{r benchmark-problem3}
set.seed(1234)

serial_time <- system.time(
  serial_result <- my_boot(
    dat = simulation_data,
    stat = my_stat,
    R = 4000,
    ncpus = 1L
  )
)

set.seed(1234)

parallel_time <- system.time(
  parallel_result <- my_boot(
    dat = simulation_data,
    stat = my_stat,
    R = 4000,
    ncpus = 2L
  )
)

serial_time
parallel_time
```

The elapsed times can be compared directly.

```{r speed-comparison}
timing_comparison <- data.frame(
  method = c("One core", "Two cores"),
  elapsed_seconds = c(
    unname(serial_time["elapsed"]),
    unname(parallel_time["elapsed"])
  )
)

timing_comparison

speedup <- unname(serial_time["elapsed"]) /
  unname(parallel_time["elapsed"])

speedup
```

A speedup value greater than 1 indicates that the two-core version was faster.
The exact performance will depend on the computer, operating system, workload,
and overhead required to create and coordinate the worker processes.
